o: Whether two names refer to the same object
Whether a value is in a list

fixed.w: A parallelogram denotes input/output; a small circle is a connector.

o: It must be written in a programming language
fixed.w: Knuth's properties: finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness. An algorithm can be written in plain language or pseudocode.

fixed.q: Pseudocode is:
o: An informal, language-independent description of an algorithm
fixed.w: Pseudocode uses structured English-like statements and is not executed.

fixed.q: The three basic control structures of structured programming are:
fixed.w: Böhm–Jacopini: any algorithm can be built from sequence, selection (if) and iteration (loops).

theory.Basics:
• Literals: 062 octal (50), 0x62 hex (98). Format: %d int, %ld long, %f float, %lf double, %c, %s, %x, %o, %u. Escapes: \a bell, \b, \n, \t, \0.
• stdio.h for printf/scanf; stdarg.h variable args. void = no params/return. printf returns characters printed.
theory.Operators:
• Integer division truncates (7/2 = 3, 7%2 = 1). ++v before use, v++ after. Modifying a variable twice in one expression is undefined.
• Precedence: postfix > unary > * / % > + − > << >> > relational > == != > & > ^ > | > && > || > ?: > = > ,. if (a = 5) is assignment (true).
theory.Control flow: • switch falls through without break. for (…); has an empty body. do-while runs at least once. while (i--) tests then decrements.
theory.Storage classes: • auto, register, static, extern (volatile is a qualifier). static local keeps its value; static/global default 0; auto holds garbage. Old C default return type int.
theory.Pointers: • a[i] = *(a + i) = i[a]. *p++ = *(p++). (*p)++ increments the value. Swap needs pointers (C is call by value). int (*f)(int*) = pointer to function.
theory.Structures: • struct size = sum of members (plus padding); union size = largest member.
theory.Macros: • Macros are text substitution: #define SQ(x) x*x → SQ(2+3) = 11. Use ((x)*(x)).
theory.Recursion: • Trace calls; base case stops recursion.
theory.Types: • Unsigned values wrap modulo 2ⁿ; signed overflow is undefined.
theory.Java & OOP:
• Java: platform independent (bytecode on the JVM), no pointers, automatic garbage collection; javac compiles, java runs.
• Primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char (16-bit Unicode), boolean. String and arrays are objects.
• Access, strictest → loosest: private, default (package), protected, public.
• final: variable constant, method cannot be overridden, class cannot be inherited. static: belongs to the class. abstract class cannot be instantiated; interfaces can have default methods (Java 8+).
• Overloading (compile time) vs overriding (run time). Java has no multiple inheritance of classes (use interfaces).
• Exceptions: try with many catch blocks but at most one finally; checked vs unchecked.
• Class loaders: Bootstrap (primordial, no parent), Extension, System/Application. Servlets run inside a web server/container.
• Integer literals starting with 0 are octal: 017 = 15.
theory.C++ & OOP:
• OOP pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism.
• class members are private by default, struct members public.
• Constructors: same name, no return type, can be overloaded, cannot be virtual. Destructor ~X(), no arguments, can be virtual.
• Compile-time polymorphism: function/operator overloading, templates. Run-time: virtual functions (late binding, vtable). Pure virtual (= 0) makes a class abstract.
• friend function accesses private members; :: scope resolution; this pointer; new/delete; references (int &r = x).
• Inheritance types: single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid (diamond problem → virtual base class).
• Operators that cannot be overloaded: ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof.
theory.Python:
• Dynamically typed, indentation defines blocks, interpreted.
• Operators: / true division (7/2 = 3.5), // floor (3), % modulo, ** power (right-associative: 2**3**2 = 512), is (identity) vs == (value), and/or/not.
• Mutable: list, dict, set. Immutable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset.
• range(start, stop, step) excludes stop. Slicing s[a:b:c]; s[::-1] reverses.
• list.append(x) adds one element; extend adds each item. dict keys must be immutable and unique.
• def, lambda, return; default arguments; *args, **kwargs.
• Pandas: Series (1-D), DataFrame (2-D); head(), tail(), describe(), read_csv(); loc (labels) vs iloc (positions).
theory.Other languages:
• FORTRAN = FORmula TRANslation (scientific, the oldest high-level language); ** is exponentiation with the highest priority, then * and /, then + and −.
• COBOL: business. LISP and Prolog: AI (Prolog is 5GL/logic). BASIC: beginners. Pascal: teaching structured programming.
• Interpreted (typically): Perl, Python, JavaScript, Ruby. Compiled: C, C++, FORTRAN.
theory.Problem solving & flowcharts:
• Algorithm properties (Knuth): finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness.
• Flowchart symbols: oval = start/stop, parallelogram = input/output, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, circle = connector, arrows = flow.
• Pseudocode: informal, language-independent.
• Structured programming (Böhm–Jacopini): sequence, selection, iteration.
• Problem-solving steps: understand, design algorithm, code, test/debug, document.
